name: NAT and PAT
author: Recurse
subject: networking
description: Configure static NAT, dynamic pools and PAT on a Cisco router, read the NAT table and fix broken translations.

lesson.intro: Almost every packet that leaves a home or office for the internet passes through NAT. Network Address Translation lets hundreds of hosts with private addresses share a few public addresses, or a single one. The CCNA tests the vocabulary (inside local, inside global and friends), the three flavors, the IOS configuration and the show commands that prove it works or reveal why it does not.
objectives: Identify the inside local, inside global, outside local and outside global addresses in a flow or a NAT table
Choose between static NAT, a dynamic pool and PAT for a given requirement
Configure static NAT, dynamic NAT and PAT with interface roles, an ACL, a pool and overload
Verify NAT with show ip nat translations and show ip nat statistics
Troubleshoot reversed interfaces, mismatched ACLs and exhausted pools

sections.title: Why NAT exists
sections.body:
Picture a small office: 40 laptops, phones and printers on 192.168.1.0/24, and one connection to an ISP that gives the office a single public address, 203.0.113.2. Everyone wants to load web pages at the same time. The problem is that 192.168.1.0/24 is a **private** range. Internet routers do not route private addresses, and even if a packet got out, the reply could never find its way back, because thousands of other networks use the very same range.

**Network Address Translation (NAT)** fixes this at the edge router. As a packet leaves the office, the router rewrites the private source address into a public one and records the swap in its **NAT translation table**. When the reply comes back to the public address, the router looks up the table, rewrites the destination back to the private address and forwards the packet inside. Neither the laptop nor the web server knows anything happened.

The private ranges from RFC 1918 are worth knowing cold, because NAT questions assume you can spot them instantly:

- `10.0.0.0/8`: 10.0.0.0 to 10.255.255.255
- `172.16.0.0/12`: 172.16.0.0 to 172.31.255.255
- `192.168.0.0/16`: 192.168.0.0 to 192.168.255.255

NAT is the main reason IPv4 survived running out of public addresses: a whole company can sit behind one public address or a handful of them. A side effect is that inside hosts cannot be reached from the internet unless a translation exists for them, which hides them a little. That is not a firewall, though. NAT does not inspect traffic or enforce a policy, it only rewrites addresses.

The CCNA blueprint topic is **inside source NAT**: translating the **source** address of packets that start on the inside and head out. The router only builds new dynamic translations for packets that arrive on an interface you marked as inside and leave through one marked as outside. Keep that rule in mind, because the most common NAT fault in labs and on the exam is getting those two interface roles backwards.
sections.code:
Inside (private)                        Outside (internet)
PC 192.168.1.10 ---[G0/1   R1   G0/0]--- ISP --- web server 198.51.100.7
                    ip nat    ip nat
                    inside    outside

Leaving:   src 192.168.1.10:51000  becomes  src 203.0.113.2:51000  (dst 198.51.100.7:443)
Returning: dst 203.0.113.2:51000   becomes  dst 192.168.1.10:51000 (src 198.51.100.7:443)

NAT table on R1
Inside local          Inside global
192.168.1.10:51000    203.0.113.2:51000
sections.tip: If the inside uses RFC 1918 addresses and needs the internet, some device on the path must do NAT.
sections.pitfall: Treating NAT as a security feature. It hides inside addresses as a side effect, but it does not filter anything. You still need ACLs or a firewall.

check.question: A host at 172.20.5.9 sends a packet to a server on the internet with no NAT on the path. What goes wrong?
choices: 172.20.5.9 is a private address, so the internet will not route it or the replies
172.20.5.9 is a public address that belongs to another company
The packet is too large to cross the ISP link without fragmentation
The server cannot answer because it does not know the host's MAC address
check.explanation: 172.16.0.0/12 runs from 172.16.0.0 to 172.31.255.255, so 172.20.5.9 is private. Internet routers do not route private ranges and replies could never come back. 172.20.x.x is a classic trap because people only remember 172.16.x.x. MAC addresses never matter beyond the local link.

sections.title: Inside local, inside global and the outside pair
sections.body:
Cisco names every address in a NAT flow with two words, and the exam leans hard on this vocabulary. Stay with the office from the last section: laptop 192.168.1.10 browses to a server at 198.51.100.7, and R1 translates the laptop to 203.0.113.2.

The first word says **where the host lives**, from the NAT router's point of view:

- **Inside**: the host is in your network (the laptop).
- **Outside**: the host is on the far side of the NAT router (the web server).

The second word says **which view of the address you are looking at**:

- **Local**: the address as it appears on the inside network.
- **Global**: the address as it appears on the outside network, the internet.

Combine them and you get four terms:

- **Inside local**: the inside host's address as seen inside. Usually private. Here, 192.168.1.10.
- **Inside global**: the inside host's address as seen on the internet, after translation. Usually public. Here, 203.0.113.2.
- **Outside global**: the outside host's real address on the internet. Here, 198.51.100.7.
- **Outside local**: the outside host's address as seen from inside. Inside source NAT never touches the destination, so outside local equals outside global (198.51.100.7). They only differ with destination NAT, which the CCNA does not test.

A memory trick from the official guide: think of inside local as "inside private" and inside global as "inside public". And if an answer choice calls the web server's address an inside anything, it is wrong: the server lives outside.

`show ip nat translations` prints all four in this order: **Inside global, Inside local, Outside local, Outside global**. The public address comes first, which trips people up when they read the output in a hurry. Read the column header every time.
sections.code:
R1# show ip nat translations
Pro Inside global       Inside local         Outside local        Outside global
tcp 203.0.113.2:51000   192.168.1.10:51000   198.51.100.7:443     198.51.100.7:443
sections.tip: Inside or outside says where the host lives. Local or global says whether you are looking from inside or from the internet.
sections.pitfall: Reading the table as local first, then global. The first address column is Inside global, the second is Inside local.

check.question: Using the output above, which value is the laptop's inside global address?
check.explanation: The inside global address is the public address the internet sees for the inside host: 203.0.113.2, here with PAT port 51000. 192.168.1.10 is the inside local address, and 198.51.100.7 is the server (outside local and outside global). 203.0.113.2:443 mixes the public address with the server's port.

sections.title: Static NAT, dynamic NAT and PAT
sections.body:
There are three ways to do inside source NAT. They differ in how inside local addresses map to inside global ones.

**Static NAT** is a fixed one-to-one mapping that you configure. 192.168.1.20 always becomes 203.0.113.6, and the entry never times out. Because the mapping exists before any traffic flows, hosts on the internet can open connections to 203.0.113.6 and reach the inside server. Use it for servers that must be reachable at a known public address. It saves no addresses: one public address per inside host.

**Dynamic NAT** uses a **pool** of public addresses. When an inside host first sends a packet that needs translation, the router takes the next free address from the pool and creates a one-to-one entry. The entry times out after a period of inactivity and the address returns to the pool. It is still one public address per active inside host, so a pool of 4 addresses supports 4 inside hosts at a time. When the pool is empty, the router **drops** packets from the next host until an entry times out or is cleared.

**PAT (Port Address Translation)**, also called **NAT overload**, translates the address and the port. Many inside hosts share one public address, and the router tells their flows apart by port number. The table holds one entry per unique inside local address and port. The port field is 16 bits, so a single public address can carry more than 65,000 simultaneous flows, which is how a whole office or home lives behind one address. If two inside hosts happen to pick the same source port, PAT simply uses a different port on the public side for the second one.

PAT is by far the most common form today. The keyword that turns dynamic NAT into PAT is `overload`, and it is the single most tested detail in the configuration.

A rough rule for choosing: a server that people on the internet must reach needs static NAT; users who only start connections outward get PAT; dynamic NAT without overload is mostly an exam topic now, but you must know how it behaves when its pool runs dry.
sections.code:
Static NAT          Dynamic NAT (pool)     PAT (overload)
Mapping          1:1, fixed          1:1, borrowed          many:1, by port
Built from       one line per host   ACL + pool             ACL + interface or pool
Entry lifetime   permanent           times out when idle    times out when idle
Internet can     yes, any time       only while an entry    only while an entry
start a flow?                        exists                 exists
Saves public     no                  a little               massively
addresses?
Typical use      public servers      rare today             every office and home
sections.pitfall: Using a dynamic pool without overload for a whole LAN. The first few hosts work, then everyone else fails silently once the pool is used up.

activity.title: Watch the translation table
activity.prompt: Send inside hosts out through static NAT, then a small pool, then PAT. Notice that the static entry exists before any traffic, that the pool runs out when more hosts than addresses want out, and that PAT keeps every flow on one public address by giving each one its own port.

check.question: A company has 200 users and one public address from its ISP, and every user needs to browse at the same time. Which NAT type fits?
choices: Static NAT, with one mapping per user
PAT, overloading the single public address
Dynamic NAT with a pool containing that one address
Destination NAT, translating the server addresses
check.explanation: Only PAT lets many hosts share one address at the same moment, by giving each flow a unique port. Static NAT would need 200 public addresses, and a one-address pool without overload serves exactly one host at a time.

sections.title: Configuring static NAT and a dynamic pool
sections.body:
Every NAT configuration has three jobs: tell the router which interfaces are inside and outside, say what to translate, and say what to translate it to. The example below uses the office router with a small block of public addresses, 203.0.113.0/29.

**Mark the interfaces.** `ip nat inside` goes on interfaces facing your private network and `ip nat outside` on the interface facing the internet. These are not optional decoration: translation only happens for traffic moving between an inside and an outside interface.

**Static NAT** needs one global command per mapping, inside local first, inside global second:

`ip nat inside source static 192.168.1.20 203.0.113.6`

Read it aloud: for hosts on the inside, translate the source address 192.168.1.20 into 203.0.113.6. The `static` keyword makes the entry permanent, so it appears in the table right away.

**Dynamic NAT** needs two more pieces. A standard ACL says which inside local addresses are eligible, and `ip nat pool` lists the inside global addresses to hand out:

- `access-list 1 permit 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255` matches every host in 192.168.1.0/24. Here the ACL is only a matching tool. Hosts it does not match are simply not translated; nothing is filtered.
- `ip nat pool PUB 203.0.113.3 203.0.113.5 netmask 255.255.255.248` defines a pool from .3 to .5 inclusive, three addresses. You can write `prefix-length 29` instead of the netmask.
- `ip nat inside source list 1 pool PUB` ties them together: packets from hosts matched by ACL 1, arriving on an inside interface, get an address from pool PUB.

IOS sanity-checks the pool. The first and last addresses must fall in the same subnet according to the mask you give, or the command is rejected. With netmask 255.255.255.252, 200.1.1.1 and 200.1.1.2 share the subnet 200.1.1.0 to 200.1.1.3, but 200.1.1.1 and 200.1.1.6 do not, so a pool from .1 to .6 with that mask fails.

Static NAT can also map a single port, which helps when you own only one public address but need an inside web server reachable on port 80: `ip nat inside source static tcp 192.168.1.20 80 203.0.113.2 80`. People often call that port forwarding.
sections.code:
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 description LAN 192.168.1.0/24
 ip address 192.168.1.1 255.255.255.0
 ip nat inside
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 description ISP, public block 203.0.113.0/29
 ip address 203.0.113.2 255.255.255.248
 ip nat outside
!
! Static: the web server is always 203.0.113.6 on the internet
ip nat inside source static 192.168.1.20 203.0.113.6
!
! Dynamic: other hosts borrow .3 to .5, one host per address
access-list 1 permit 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255
ip nat pool PUB 203.0.113.3 203.0.113.5 netmask 255.255.255.248
ip nat inside source list 1 pool PUB
sections.tip: The NAT ACL selects traffic for translation. It does not permit or deny anything on an interface.
sections.pitfall: Reversing the static mapping. The order is inside local, then inside global. Swapped, the router waits for a private host at the public address and never translates the real server.

check.question: Which command creates a pool of inside global addresses from 198.51.100.65 to 198.51.100.70?
choices: ip nat inside source list 1 pool WEB 198.51.100.65 198.51.100.70
ip nat outside source pool WEB 198.51.100.65 198.51.100.70
check.explanation: ip nat pool takes a name, a first address, a last address and a mask. With 255.255.255.248 (/29), .65 and .70 sit in the same subnet (.64 to .71), so IOS accepts it. With a /30 mask they fall in different subnets and IOS rejects the command. The ip nat inside source command references a pool by name; it does not define one.

sections.title: Configuring PAT (overload)
sections.body:
PAT reuses the dynamic NAT building blocks and adds one keyword. There are two variations, and both show up on the exam.

**PAT on the outside interface's own address.** This is what nearly every branch and home router does: the ISP gives you one address, it sits on the outside interface, and everyone shares it.

`ip nat inside source list 1 interface GigabitEthernet0/0 overload`

Read it aloud: hosts matching ACL 1 that arrive on an inside interface are translated to the address of G0/0, and `overload` means share that address using ports. No pool is needed. A bonus: if G0/0 learns a new address from the ISP through DHCP, PAT follows it automatically.

**PAT on a pool.** If you have a few public addresses, put them in a pool and overload it:

`ip nat inside source list 1 pool PUB overload`

Remove `overload` from that line and you are back to plain dynamic NAT, one host per pool address. That one word is the difference between 3 users online and 3,000.

The full PAT build for the classic exam topology is below. The order you type the pieces in does not matter, but all four must exist: the inside interface, the outside interface, the ACL, and the ip nat inside source rule. The ACL number in the rule must match the ACL you actually wrote, and the interface named in the rule should be the outside one.

In the translation table, PAT entries are easy to spot: the Pro column shows tcp, udp or icmp, and every address has a port after it. Static and one-to-one dynamic entries show `---` instead, because they translate the whole address.
sections.code:
R1(config)# interface GigabitEthernet0/1
R1(config-if)# ip nat inside
R1(config-if)# interface GigabitEthernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ip nat outside
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# access-list 1 permit 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255
R1(config)# ip nat inside source list 1 interface GigabitEthernet0/0 overload
sections.pitfall: Forgetting overload. IOS accepts the command and the first host works, which makes the mistake easy to miss in a lab and painful in production.

activity.title: Lab: PAT to the internet
activity.prompt: Build PAT on R1. G0/1 faces the 192.168.1.0/24 LAN and G0/0 faces the internet. Mark the inside and outside interfaces, match the LAN with access-list 1, then overload it onto G0/0. Finish with show ip nat statistics and confirm which interface it lists as inside and which as outside.

check.question: A router has `ip nat inside source list 1 pool PUB` with a 3-address pool, and only 3 users can browse at a time. What is the simplest fix?
choices: Add the overload keyword to the ip nat inside source command
Move ip nat inside to the outside interface
Change access-list 1 to an extended ACL
Add a static NAT entry for each user
check.explanation: Without overload, each pool address serves one inside host at a time, so 3 addresses means 3 users. Adding overload turns the rule into PAT and lets everyone share the pool by port. Static entries would need one public address per user, which is exactly what is missing.

sections.title: Verifying NAT
sections.body:
Two show commands prove NAT is working, and exam exhibits use both.

`show ip nat translations` lists the NAT table. Static entries appear as soon as you configure them, with `---` in the protocol and port positions. Dynamic entries only appear after inside traffic triggers them, so an empty table right after you finish typing usually just means nobody has sent anything yet. Generate traffic (a ping from an inside host) and look again.

`show ip nat statistics` gives the big picture:

- **Total active translations**, split into static, dynamic and extended. Extended entries carry ports, so they are PAT.
- **Outside interfaces** and **Inside interfaces**: the fastest way to catch reversed `ip nat inside` and `ip nat outside` commands.
- **Hits** and **Misses**: a hit is a packet that used an existing entry. A miss is a packet that needed translation and found no entry, so the router tried to build one. A few misses with many hits is normal: each new flow starts with a miss.
- For a pool: total addresses, how many are **allocated** (with a percentage) and a second **misses** counter. This one only grows when the router wanted to build a translation and found no free pool address. Allocated 100% and a growing pool misses counter is the signature of pool exhaustion.

`clear ip nat translation *` deletes all **dynamic** entries. Static mappings stay, because they come from the configuration. It is handy after a change, when you want to test from a clean table instead of waiting for idle entries to time out. You can also clear a single entry by naming its addresses.

`debug ip nat` prints a line for every translated packet, such as `NAT*: s=192.168.1.10->203.0.113.2, d=198.51.100.7`. Great in a lab, risky on a busy production router.
sections.code:
R1# show ip nat translations
Pro Inside global        Inside local         Outside local        Outside global
--- 203.0.113.6          192.168.1.20         ---                  ---
tcp 203.0.113.2:49712    192.168.1.10:49712   198.51.100.7:443     198.51.100.7:443
tcp 203.0.113.2:49713    192.168.1.11:49713   198.51.100.7:443     198.51.100.7:443
udp 203.0.113.2:53001    192.168.1.12:53001   8.8.8.8:53           8.8.8.8:53

R1# show ip nat statistics
Total active translations: 4 (1 static, 3 dynamic; 3 extended)
Peak translations: 9, occurred 00:04:12 ago
Outside interfaces:
  GigabitEthernet0/0
Inside interfaces:
  GigabitEthernet0/1
Hits: 1486  Misses: 37
Expired translations: 31
Dynamic mappings:
-- Inside Source
[Id: 1] access-list 1 interface GigabitEthernet0/0 refcount 3
sections.tip: Before blaming the configuration, make sure an inside host has actually sent traffic. NAT reacts to packets; it does nothing in advance except for static entries.
sections.pitfall: Expecting clear ip nat translation * to remove static mappings. Only dynamic entries are cleared; remove a static mapping with the no form of its configuration command.

check.question: A pool line in show ip nat statistics reads `total addresses 4, allocated 4 (100%), misses 212`, and the misses number keeps climbing. What does it mean?
choices: The ACL is not matching any inside hosts
212 packets were translated successfully using the pool
Every pool address is in use and new hosts are failing to get a translation
The inside and outside interfaces are reversed
check.explanation: The pool misses counter only grows when the router needs a new translation and has no free address left. With 100% allocated, extra hosts are dropped. Adding overload or more addresses fixes it. Successful translations count as hits, not misses.

sections.title: Troubleshooting NAT
sections.body:
Most NAT problems are configuration mistakes, and the same handful show up in labs, in production and in exam simulations. Work through them in this order.

- **Inside and outside reversed.** Source NAT only builds new translations for packets that arrive on an inside interface and leave through an outside interface. Swap the roles and nothing translates. Check the Inside interfaces and Outside interfaces lists in `show ip nat statistics`.
- **The ACL matches the wrong addresses.** It must match the inside local (private) source addresses, the way packets look before translation. An ACL that permits the public range, the wrong subnet, or uses a bad wildcard (0.0.0.0 instead of 0.0.0.255) leaves hosts untranslated. `show access-lists` shows whether its counters move.
- **Wrong ACL number or pool name.** `ip nat inside source list 2` when you wrote access-list 1 matches nothing. A typo in a pool name has the same effect.
- **Pool exhausted or overload missing.** All pool addresses allocated and the pool misses counter rising. Add `overload` or more addresses.
- **Static mapping reversed.** Inside local first, inside global second.
- **An interface ACL drops the traffic.** For packets entering an interface, IOS checks the inbound ACL before NAT, so an inbound ACL on the inside interface sees private addresses. For packets leaving an interface, NAT runs first, so an outbound ACL on the outside interface sees the translated public address.
- **Routing.** R1 needs a route toward the internet (usually a default route) and the ISP must route your inside global addresses back to you. NAT cannot fix a missing route.

A quick routine: send traffic from an inside host, then run `show ip nat statistics` (are the interface roles right, are hits and misses moving?), `show ip nat translations` (does the host appear?) and `show access-lists` (is the NAT ACL matching?). The exhibit below is the most common failure of all. Look at which interface faces the LAN and which role it has.
sections.code:
R1# show running-config
! output trimmed
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 description ISP
 ip address 203.0.113.2 255.255.255.248
 ip nat inside
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 description LAN
 ip address 192.168.1.1 255.255.255.0
 ip nat outside
access-list 1 permit 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255
ip nat inside source list 1 interface GigabitEthernet0/0 overload

R1# show ip nat statistics
Total active translations: 0 (0 static, 0 dynamic; 0 extended)
Outside interfaces:
  GigabitEthernet0/1
Inside interfaces:
  GigabitEthernet0/0
Hits: 0  Misses: 0
sections.pitfall: Writing the NAT ACL with the public addresses because that is what reaches the internet. NAT matches packets before translation, so the ACL must list the private inside local addresses.

activity.title: Troubleshoot: NAT translates nothing
activity.prompt: PAT is configured on R1 but inside hosts cannot reach the internet. Start with show ip nat statistics and read which interface is listed as inside and which as outside. Fix the roles (no ip nat outside then ip nat inside on G0/1, and the reverse on G0/0), then check the statistics again.

check.question: Using the exhibit above, why are the LAN hosts not being translated?
choices: ACL 1 uses the wrong wildcard mask for a /24
The ip nat inside and ip nat outside commands are on the wrong interfaces
The overload keyword cannot be used with an interface
PAT requires a pool to be named in the ip nat inside source command
check.explanation: G0/1 faces the 192.168.1.0/24 LAN but is marked outside, and G0/0 faces the ISP but is marked inside. Source NAT only translates traffic that arrives on an inside interface, so LAN traffic never triggers a translation. Swap the two commands. The ACL and the PAT rule are both correct.

keyTerms.definition: Network Address Translation: a router rewrites IP addresses as packets cross it, usually private to public on the way out and back again on the way in.
The inside host's address as seen on the inside network, normally a private RFC 1918 address.
The inside host's address as seen on the internet after translation, normally public.
The outside host's real address on the internet. Inside source NAT never changes it.
The outside host's address as seen from the inside. Equal to outside global unless destination NAT is used.
A permanent one-to-one mapping between an inside local and an inside global address, configured by hand.
One-to-one translation using addresses borrowed from a pool for inside hosts matched by an ACL; entries time out when idle.
Many inside hosts share one inside global address, told apart by translated port numbers. Enabled with the overload keyword.
A range of inside global addresses defined with ip nat pool name first last netmask mask.
The router's list of active mappings, shown with show ip nat translations.

summary: NAT rewrites private inside local addresses into public inside global ones at the edge and records each swap in the translation table.
Static NAT is a permanent one-to-one mapping for servers, dynamic NAT lends one pool address per active host, and PAT shares one address among many hosts by port.
Configure ip nat inside and ip nat outside on the interfaces, an ACL that matches the private sources, then ip nat inside source static, list ... pool, or list ... interface ... overload.
The overload keyword is what makes PAT; without it a small pool runs out and extra hosts are dropped.
Verify with show ip nat translations and show ip nat statistics; clear ip nat translation * removes dynamic entries only.
Most faults are reversed interface roles, an ACL that does not match the inside local addresses, an exhausted pool or a reversed static mapping.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend how fifty phones in a coffee shop can all browse the web through one public IP address, and how the router knows which phone each reply belongs to. Use the terms inside local, inside global and PAT.

questions.question: R1 translates PC1 (192.168.10.5) to 198.51.100.10 when PC1 browses to a server at 203.0.113.80. Which address is PC1's inside local address?
choices: The address of R1's inside interface
questions.explanation: Inside local is the inside host's address as seen on the inside network, usually its private address: 192.168.10.5. 198.51.100.10 is PC1's inside global address, and 203.0.113.80 is the server's outside global address.

questions.question: Match each NAT term to its meaning.

pairs.right: The inside host's address as seen on the inside, usually private
The inside host's address as seen on the internet after translation
The outside host's real address on the internet
The outside host's address as seen from the inside network

questions.explanation: Inside or outside says where the host lives; local or global says which side you are looking from. With inside source NAT the destination is never changed, so outside local and outside global hold the same value.

questions.question: Based on the exhibit, which statement is correct?
questions.code:
R1# show ip nat translations
Pro Inside global       Inside local        Outside local       Outside global
tcp 198.51.100.2:1050   10.1.1.25:1050      203.0.113.9:80      203.0.113.9:80
choices: 10.1.1.25 is the inside global address
203.0.113.9 is the inside local address of the web server
10.1.1.25 is the outside local address
198.51.100.2 is the source address the web server sees
questions.explanation: The first address column is Inside global: 198.51.100.2, the public address the server sees as the source. 10.1.1.25 is the inside local address. 203.0.113.9 is the server, an outside host, so it can never be an inside address.

questions.question: How does PAT let many inside hosts share one inside global address at the same time?
choices: It gives each flow a unique port on the inside global address
It queues hosts and lets them use the address one at a time
It gives each host a different MAC address on the outside interface
It encrypts each host's traffic with a separate key
questions.explanation: PAT translates the source port as well as the address and keeps one table entry per inside address and port, so replies to each port go back to the right host. Nothing is queued or encrypted, and MAC addresses never leave the local link.

questions.question: A router runs dynamic NAT without overload, using a pool of 4 addresses. Four inside hosts are browsing. What happens when a fifth host sends a packet to the internet?
choices: The router gives the fifth host a port on one of the four addresses
The router forwards the packet with its private source address
The router drops the packet until a pool address is freed
The router removes the oldest translation to make room
questions.explanation: Without overload each active host holds one pool address. With all four in use there is nothing to allocate, so the router drops the fifth host's packets until an entry times out or is cleared. Sharing addresses by port only happens with overload.

questions.question: Which two statements about static NAT are true? (Choose two.)
choices: The mapping is permanent and does not time out
Hosts on the internet can start connections to the inside host
Many inside hosts can share one public address
An ACL is required to choose which hosts are translated
Its entries appear only after the inside host sends traffic
questions.explanation: A static mapping comes from the configuration, so it is always in the table and never times out. That is exactly why outside hosts can reach the server at any time. Sharing one address is PAT, ACLs belong to dynamic NAT and PAT, and waiting for traffic is dynamic behavior.

questions.question: You are in interface configuration mode on R1's LAN interface. Type the command that makes it a NAT inside interface.
questions.explanation: ip nat inside marks interfaces facing the private network; ip nat outside marks the internet-facing interface. Source NAT translates traffic that enters an inside interface and leaves an outside one.

questions.question: Type the global configuration command that permanently maps inside host 10.1.1.20 to public address 198.51.100.20.
questions.explanation: The syntax is ip nat inside source static inside-local inside-global. The private address comes first. Reversing them is a classic mistake that leaves the real host untranslated.

questions.question: Type the command that creates a NAT pool named NET holding 203.0.113.17 through 203.0.113.30, with the mask written as a netmask for a /28.
questions.explanation: ip nat pool takes a name, the first and last addresses (inclusive) and a mask. A /28 is 255.255.255.240, and .17 and .30 both fall in 203.0.113.16/28, so IOS accepts it. The prefix-length 28 form is equivalent.

questions.question: Type the global command that translates hosts matched by access list 1 to the address of interface GigabitEthernet0/0, using PAT.
questions.answer: ip nat inside source list 1 interface GigabitEthernet0/0 overload
accept: ip nat inside source list 1 interface g0/0 overload
ip nat inside source list 1 interface gi0/0 overload
ip nat inside source list 1 interface gig0/0 overload
questions.explanation: list 1 picks the inside local addresses, interface GigabitEthernet0/0 makes that interface's address the inside global address, and overload turns on PAT. Without overload only one host at a time could use the address.

questions.question: About 300 inside hosts must reach the internet at the same time using only the two pool addresses. What completes the last line?
questions.code:
access-list 1 permit 10.1.0.0 0.0.255.255
ip nat pool PUB 198.51.100.1 198.51.100.2 netmask 255.255.255.252
ip nat inside source list 1 pool PUB _____
choices: static
permit
overload
extendable
questions.explanation: overload makes the pool rule PAT, so 300 hosts can share two addresses by port. Without it, only two hosts at a time could be translated. static and extendable belong to static NAT commands, and permit belongs in the ACL.

questions.question: What is the practical difference between `ip nat inside source list 1 interface G0/0 overload` and `ip nat inside source list 1 pool PUB overload`?
choices: The first performs static NAT and the second performs PAT
The first translates destinations and the second translates sources
The first needs no ip nat outside command and the second does
The first shares G0/0's own address, the second shares the addresses in pool PUB
questions.explanation: Both are PAT on inside source addresses. The only difference is where the inside global addresses come from: the outside interface's own address, or a configured pool. Both still need ip nat inside and ip nat outside on the interfaces.

questions.question: Put the steps of a PAT translation in order, from the inside host's first packet to the reply reaching it.
items: R1 receives it on an ip nat inside interface and the source matches the NAT ACL
R1 sends the packet out its ip nat outside interface from 203.0.113.2:51000
R1 finds the entry and rewrites the destination to 192.168.1.10:51000
questions.explanation: Translation is triggered by a packet entering an inside interface and matching the ACL. The router records the mapping, rewrites the source on the way out, and uses the same entry in reverse to rewrite the destination of the reply.

questions.question: Users report that only some people can reach the internet. Based on the exhibit, what is the most likely cause and fix?
questions.code:
R1# show ip nat statistics
Total active translations: 4 (0 static, 4 dynamic; 0 extended)
Peak translations: 4, occurred 00:12:09 ago
Outside interfaces:
  GigabitEthernet0/0
Inside interfaces:
  GigabitEthernet0/1
Hits: 2311  Misses: 41
Expired translations: 6
Dynamic mappings:
-- Inside Source
[Id: 1] access-list 1 pool PUB refcount 4
 pool PUB: netmask 255.255.255.248
        start 203.0.113.9 end 203.0.113.12
        type generic, total addresses 4, allocated 4 (100%), misses 37
choices: The interfaces are reversed; swap ip nat inside and ip nat outside
The pool is exhausted; add overload to the ip nat inside source command
ACL 1 matches nothing; correct the ACL wildcard mask
The pool mask is invalid; change it to 255.255.255.252
questions.explanation: All 4 pool addresses are allocated (100%) and the pool misses counter is at 37, so new hosts cannot get a translation. 0 extended translations confirms there is no PAT. Adding overload lets everyone share the pool. The interfaces are listed correctly and the ACL clearly matches, since 4 hosts are translated.

questions.question: Hosts on 10.1.1.0/24 are not being translated. What is wrong with this configuration?
questions.code:
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 ip address 10.1.1.1 255.255.255.0
 ip nat inside
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 198.51.100.2 255.255.255.252
 ip nat outside
!
access-list 1 permit 198.51.100.0 0.0.0.3
ip nat inside source list 1 interface GigabitEthernet0/0 overload
choices: The NAT roles on G0/0 and G0/1 are reversed
The overload keyword is missing
ACL 1 matches the outside subnet instead of the inside local addresses
A /30 outside interface cannot be used for PAT
questions.explanation: The NAT ACL must match the inside local (private) source addresses as packets arrive on the inside interface: access-list 1 permit 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255. It currently matches 198.51.100.0/30, which no inside host uses. The interface roles and the overload keyword are correct.

questions.question: Internet users must reach the web server 10.1.1.80 at 198.51.100.5, but connections fail. What is the bug?
questions.code:
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 ip address 10.1.1.1 255.255.255.0
 ip nat inside
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 198.51.100.2 255.255.255.248
 ip nat outside
!
ip nat inside source static 198.51.100.5 10.1.1.80
choices: The static mapping is reversed; it should be ip nat inside source static 10.1.1.80 198.51.100.5
Static NAT also needs an access list that permits 10.1.1.80
Static NAT needs the overload keyword to accept inbound connections
The server must be configured with ip nat outside source static instead
questions.explanation: The command takes the inside local address first and the inside global second. As written, the router maps a nonexistent inside host 198.51.100.5 to 10.1.1.80, so the real server is never translated. Static NAT needs no ACL and no overload.

questions.question: An engineer runs `clear ip nat translation *` on a router with two static mappings and 50 PAT entries. What is in the table immediately afterward?
choices: Nothing; every entry is removed
Only the PAT entries that are carrying traffic
All entries; the command only resets the counters
Only the two static mappings
questions.explanation: The command removes dynamic entries only. Static mappings come from the running configuration and stay in the table. PAT entries are rebuilt as soon as hosts send new traffic.

questions.question: How many inside global addresses does this pool provide? `ip nat pool P 203.0.113.33 203.0.113.38 netmask 255.255.255.248`
questions.explanation: The range is inclusive: .33, .34, .35, .36, .37 and .38 make 6 addresses. The netmask is only a sanity check that both ends fall in the same subnet (203.0.113.32/29); it does not add the rest of the subnet to the pool.

questions.question: An engineer enters `ip nat pool P 200.1.1.1 200.1.1.6 netmask 255.255.255.252` and IOS rejects it. Why?
choices: Pools must contain an even number of addresses
With a /30 mask, 200.1.1.1 and 200.1.1.6 fall in different subnets
The netmask must match the outside interface's mask exactly
Pool names must be at least three characters long
questions.explanation: IOS checks that the first and last addresses share a subnet under the given mask. With /30, 200.1.1.1 is in 200.1.1.0/30 and 200.1.1.6 is in 200.1.1.4/30, so the pool is rejected. A mask of 255.255.255.248 would work.

questions.question: In show ip nat statistics, what does the first Misses counter (the one next to Hits) count?
choices: Packets dropped because the NAT pool was empty
Packets that did not match the NAT access list
Translations that expired because they were idle
Packets that needed translation, found no existing entry, so the router tried to build one
questions.explanation: Each new flow starts with a miss: the packet needed NAT, no entry existed, and the router created one. Later packets in the flow are hits. Pool exhaustion is counted by the separate misses counter on the pool line, and expired entries have their own counter.

questions.question: A company hosts a web server inside at 10.1.1.80 and wants internet users to always reach it at 198.51.100.80. Which NAT type should it use for the server?
choices: PAT on the outside interface
Dynamic NAT from a pool
Static NAT
No NAT; publish 10.1.1.80 in DNS
questions.explanation: Inbound connections need a mapping that exists before any traffic and never changes, which is static NAT. PAT and dynamic entries only exist after the inside host sends traffic, and 10.1.1.80 is private, so it is unreachable from the internet.

questions.question: You finish configuring dynamic NAT in a lab and show ip nat translations shows no entries. What is the most likely reason?
choices: No inside host has sent traffic that needs translation yet
Dynamic entries are only shown by show ip nat statistics
The router must be reloaded before NAT takes effect
The pool command was rejected for being too small
questions.explanation: Dynamic NAT and PAT build entries in reaction to traffic entering an inside interface. Send a ping from an inside host to an outside address and the entry appears. No reload is needed.

questions.question: R1 must run PAT using the address of its internet-facing interface. Which items are required? (Choose all that apply.)
choices: ip nat inside on the LAN interface
ip nat outside on the internet-facing interface
An access list matching the inside local addresses
An ip nat pool command
ip nat inside source list ... interface ... overload
An ip nat inside source static command for each host
questions.explanation: PAT on an interface needs the two interface roles, an ACL to select inside hosts and the rule that names the interface with overload. A pool is only needed when you overload a range of addresses, and static entries are a different NAT type.

questions.question: What is the difference between dynamic NAT and PAT?
questions.answer: Dynamic NAT gives each active inside host its own public address from a pool, one to one, so the pool size limits how many hosts can be online at once. PAT (overload) lets many hosts share one public address by translating source ports too.
questions.explanation: The key idea is one-to-one versus many-to-one. The overload keyword is what turns the first into the second.

questions.question: Roughly how many simultaneous flows can PAT carry on a single inside global address?
choices: About 254, one per host address in a /24
More than 65,000, because the port field is 16 bits
About 1,024, the well-known port range
Exactly 4,096, the size of the NAT table
questions.explanation: PAT tells flows apart by port, and TCP and UDP ports are 16-bit numbers, so one address offers more than 65,000 ports. That is why one public address can serve a large office.

questions.question: What does the exhibit show?
choices: Three inside hosts using static NAT
Two inside hosts sharing one inside global address with PAT, one of them with two connections
Two inside hosts each using a separate pool address
One inside host with three translations from a dynamic pool
questions.explanation: The inside local column shows two hosts (10.1.1.11 and 10.1.1.12, the second with two flows), all translated to the same inside global address with different ports. Ports and the tcp protocol mark these as PAT entries; static entries would show --- instead.

questions.question: R1 has an inbound ACL on its inside interface G0/1 and performs PAT out G0/0. Which source addresses must that inbound ACL permit for the LAN traffic to pass?
choices: The inside local addresses, because inbound ACLs are checked before NAT
The inside global address, because NAT happens before the ACL
Either one, because IOS checks the ACL against both
The outside global addresses of the destination servers
questions.explanation: For packets entering an interface, IOS applies the inbound ACL before NAT, so it sees the private inside local source. The opposite holds outbound: an outbound ACL on the outside interface is checked after translation and sees the inside global address.

questions.question: Type the command that displays the NAT translation table.
questions.explanation: show ip nat translations lists every static and dynamic entry with its inside global, inside local, outside local and outside global addresses.

questions.question: Type the command that removes all dynamic NAT translations from the table.
questions.explanation: clear ip nat translation * deletes every dynamic entry. Static mappings stay because they come from the configuration.

questions.question: G0/1 connects to the LAN and G0/0 to the ISP. Users cannot reach the internet. Which change fixes the problem?
questions.code:
R1# show ip nat statistics
Total active translations: 0 (0 static, 0 dynamic; 0 extended)
Outside interfaces:
  GigabitEthernet0/1
Inside interfaces:
  GigabitEthernet0/0
Hits: 0  Misses: 0
Dynamic mappings:
-- Inside Source
[Id: 1] access-list 1 interface GigabitEthernet0/0 refcount 0
choices: Add the overload keyword to the ip nat inside source command
Change the rule to use a pool instead of the interface address
Add ip nat inside to G0/0 so both interfaces are inside
Make G0/1 ip nat inside and G0/0 ip nat outside, removing the old roles
questions.explanation: The statistics list the LAN interface G0/1 as outside and the ISP interface G0/0 as inside, so LAN traffic never enters an inside interface and nothing is translated. Swapping the roles fixes it. Hits and misses at 0 confirm NAT has never even tried.

questions.question: Which source address would need NAT to reach the internet?
questions.explanation: 172.16.0.0/12 covers 172.16.0.0 to 172.31.255.255, so 172.31.200.4 is private. 172.32.0.4 is just outside that block, 11.0.0.1 is outside 10.0.0.0/8, and 192.169.1.1 is outside 192.168.0.0/16. All three of those are public.

questions.question: What does inside source NAT change in a packet leaving the inside network?
choices: The destination IP address
The source MAC address only
The source IP address, and with PAT the source port
The TTL and checksum only
questions.explanation: Inside source NAT rewrites the source IP address (and the source port for PAT) on the way out, then reverses it on the reply. Any router changes MAC addresses and the TTL when forwarding, but that is normal routing, not NAT.
